Direct aim: Carry and place a tray with controlled movement.
Materials: Small tray; two stable, light objects
Readiness: Can walk steadily and attend to a short demonstration.
Presentation outline: Hold opposite sides with two hands. / Walk slowly to a clear table and lower the tray quietly. / Return the tray and invite the child to try.
Point of interest: Keeping the tray level.
Feedback / control of error: Objects shift when the tray tilts.
What to observe: Grip, balance, walking pace and placement.
Possible next invitation: Carry a tray with an empty pitcher.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Lesson: Rolling and unrolling a work rug
Direct aim: Prepare and restore a defined floor workspace.
Materials: Small washable rug; open floor space
Readiness: Can grasp with both hands.
Presentation outline: Unroll the rug slowly in a clear space. / Kneel at the short edge and turn a small fold evenly. / Roll with both hands and return it to its place.
Point of interest: Matching the two edges.
Feedback / control of error: Uneven edges show where the roll wandered.
What to observe: Chooses a clear space; rolls and stores the rug.
Possible next invitation: Walk around another person’s work.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Transfer dry material by pouring with controlled starts and stops.
Materials: Two small pitchers; large dry items; tray
Readiness: Can grasp a pitcher and carry a tray.
Presentation outline: Show the starting and receiving pitchers. / Pour slowly, stopping before the second pitcher overflows. / Return spills to the tray and reset the work.
Point of interest: Starting and stopping the flow.
Feedback / control of error: Spills and items left in the starting pitcher are visible.
What to observe: Grip, wrist control and response to spills.
Possible next invitation: Pour a small amount of water.
Safety and access: Use large nonfood items if mouthing is possible. Assess choking risk and supervise; do not use beans with children who mouth objects.

Direct aim: Transfer water and manage small spills with growing independence.
Materials: Two small pitchers; a little water; tray; sponge
Readiness: Has practiced controlling a dry pour.
Presentation outline: Lift the pitcher with a steady grip and aim at the opening. / Pour slowly and stop before the container fills. / Set it down and sponge up spills.
Point of interest: The stream entering the opening.
Feedback / control of error: Water outside the pitcher is visible.
What to observe: Flow control, stopping and cleanup without distress.
Possible next invitation: Pour to a marked line.
Safety and access: Use room-temperature water and immediately dry wet floors.

Direct aim: Transfer objects with a spoon using coordinated movement.
Materials: Two bowls; spoon; large transfer objects; tray
Readiness: Can grasp and release a spoon.
Presentation outline: Place the bowls and spoon within easy reach. / Scoop, move over the receiving bowl and tip gently. / Continue, collect spills and reset.
Point of interest: Keeping the spoon level.
Feedback / control of error: A missed transfer is visible on the tray.
What to observe: Hand control and whether the spoon suits the child.
Possible next invitation: Transfer with child-sized tongs.
Safety and access: Select objects that are safe for this child; assess mouthing and choking risk.

Direct aim: Transfer objects by controlling the grip and release of tongs.
Materials: Easy-squeeze tongs; large soft objects; two bowls
Readiness: Can squeeze and release with one hand.
Presentation outline: Open the tongs around one object. / Squeeze gently, move it and release over the other bowl. / Continue and return the work in order.
Point of interest: Squeezing enough to hold without crushing.
Feedback / control of error: A dropped object shows that the grip needs adjustment.
What to observe: Grip, release and willingness to adjust.
Possible next invitation: Use tongs in snack preparation.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Carry out an effective handwashing routine with appropriate adult support.
Materials: Accessible sink; soap; safe drying method
Readiness: Can reach the setup with safe support.
Presentation outline: Wet hands, apply soap and rub all hand surfaces. / Use the program’s health guidance for thorough washing and rinsing. / Dry hands and leave the sink ready for the next person.
Point of interest: Washing between fingers and over thumbs.
Feedback / control of error: Soap or water left on hands can be seen or felt; cleanliness still requires adult guidance.
What to observe: Sequence and support needed at transitions.
Possible next invitation: Use the sequence before food and after toileting.
Safety and access: Provide safe access and supervision. Follow applicable health rules; this lesson does not replace required hygiene procedures.

Direct aim: Fasten and unfasten buttons using coordinated hands.
Materials: Buttoning frame with large buttons
Readiness: Interested in fastening; can coordinate both hands.
Presentation outline: Hold the fabric near one button. / Guide the button through the opening and draw the fabric flat. / Repeat slowly, then show how to undo it.
Point of interest: Turning the button to fit the hole.
Feedback / control of error: Misaligned edges or an unfastened button are visible.
What to observe: Two-hand coordination and persistence.
Possible next invitation: Use the skill on the child’s own clothing.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Join and separate a zipper with controlled two-hand movement.
Materials: Separating zipper frame
Readiness: Can stabilize one side while moving the other.
Presentation outline: Show the bottom pieces meeting. / Insert the pin fully while holding the slider steady. / Pull the slider upward, then reverse and separate.
Point of interest: Seating the pin before pulling.
Feedback / control of error: The zipper will not close smoothly if it is not seated.
What to observe: Whether the child needs help starting or only pulling.
Possible next invitation: Practice on a coat with permission.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Care for a table through a complete orderly cleaning sequence.
Materials: Small basin; water; cloth; mild approved soap; drying cloth
Readiness: Can carry water with support and follow a short sequence.
Presentation outline: Prepare the table and wet the cloth. / Wash in an orderly pattern, rinse and wipe. / Dry the surface and restore all materials.
Point of interest: Seeing where the cloth has already traveled.
Feedback / control of error: Visible wet or soapy patches guide another wipe.
What to observe: Order, coordination and restoring the workspace.
Possible next invitation: Invite a child to care for a shared snack table.
Safety and access: Use approved products and safe water amounts. Adults handle disinfectants and required sanitation.

Direct aim: Gather a small safe spill using a broom and dustpan.
Materials: Child-sized broom; dustpan; large safe debris
Readiness: Can manage a broom without hitting others.
Presentation outline: Mark or notice the small area to gather. / Sweep inward with controlled strokes. / Hold the pan, collect debris and return tools.
Point of interest: Bringing scattered pieces to one place.
Feedback / control of error: Pieces left on the floor remain visible.
What to observe: Tool control and checking the area afterward.
Possible next invitation: Sweep a larger defined area.
Safety and access: Keep others clear. Adults handle broken glass, bodily fluids and hazardous spills.

Direct aim: Prepare and serve a simple snack using safe routines.
Materials: Washed soft fruit; safe spreading tool; plate; handwashing access
Readiness: Can follow food hygiene routines with supervision.
Presentation outline: Wash hands and prepare a clean work area. / Demonstrate one safe preparation action slowly. / Serve an appropriate portion and clean the workspace.
Point of interest: A careful, useful action that produces food to share.
Feedback / control of error: Uneven portions can be compared; food safety needs adult oversight.
What to observe: Hygiene, tool use, portion awareness and cleanup.
Possible next invitation: Prepare a snack with a peer.
Safety and access: Check allergies and choking risks. An adult supervises tools and follows food safety rules; never use a tasting activity as an allergy test.

Direct aim: Offer an invitation and respect another person’s decision.
Materials: Two willing participants; optional role-play puppets
Readiness: Can communicate through words, signs or another supported method.
Presentation outline: Approach without touching another person’s work. / Offer a simple invitation and wait. / Model accepting either answer calmly and choosing another activity.
Point of interest: Waiting for the other person’s choice.
Feedback / control of error: The other person’s response provides feedback; an adult supports interpretation.
What to observe: Consent, waiting and alternate communication.
Possible next invitation: Practice joining play at a natural pause.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Take part in a supported, respectful solution to a disagreement.
Materials: Quiet space; optional feeling cards
Readiness: Can take a short turn with adult support; feels safe.
Presentation outline: Describe what happened without blame and ensure safety. / Invite each child’s account without forcing speech or an apology. / Offer workable choices, agree on a next step and check back.
Point of interest: Listening to different accounts.
Feedback / control of error: The agreed solution is checked in real use; adult guidance remains necessary.
What to observe: Words used, adult support and whether the solution worked.
Possible next invitation: Practice a calm request before a conflict escalates.
Safety and access: Stop aggression and protect children first. Do not require a child to mediate bullying or unsafe behavior.

Direct aim: Visually grade cubes by changing size.
Materials: Ten graded cubes; work rug
Readiness: Can carry a cube safely and compare noticeably different sizes.
Presentation outline: Carry cubes one at a time and spread them on the rug. / Build from largest to smallest with deliberate placement. / Compare the completed tower and return cubes in order.
Point of interest: Centering each smaller cube.
Feedback / control of error: The visual sequence and stability reveal many size errors.
What to observe: Compares size, carries carefully and notices changes.
Possible next invitation: Grade three cubes with a larger contrast first.
Safety and access: Never stack above a safe working height or allow cubes to be thrown.

Direct aim: Visually grade prisms by thickness.
Materials: Ten graded prisms; rug
Readiness: Has compared size; can lift the larger prisms safely.
Presentation outline: Lay prisms apart where all can be seen. / Arrange thickest to thinnest with ends aligned. / Look along the stair and restore the set.
Point of interest: Equal length with changing thickness.
Feedback / control of error: An uneven progression is visible.
What to observe: Discriminates thickness rather than overall length.
Possible next invitation: Compare thick and thin using two contrasting prisms.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Visually grade rods by length.
Materials: Graded length rods; large clear rug
Readiness: Can carry a long object safely and has space to work.
Presentation outline: Carry one rod horizontally with awareness of others. / Arrange longest to shortest with one end aligned. / Trace the changing lengths and return rods carefully.
Point of interest: Finding the next length.
Feedback / control of error: Misordered ends interrupt the visible progression.
What to observe: Length comparison and safe spatial awareness.
Possible next invitation: Build a sequence with fewer widely different rods.
Safety and access: Keep a generous clear space; adult help may be needed with long rods.

Direct aim: Match cylinder dimensions with corresponding openings.
Materials: One cylinder block; stable table
Readiness: Can use the knob comfortably.
Presentation outline: Remove cylinders with a light grasp and place them randomly. / Choose one, compare its size with a hole and lower it gently. / Continue, then invite repetition.
Point of interest: A cylinder fitting flush in its opening.
Feedback / control of error: A cylinder may not fit, or another is left without its matching opening.
What to observe: Visual comparison, grip and gentle handling.
Possible next invitation: Introduce a second block after sustained interest.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Match identical colors before emphasizing color names.
Materials: A small set of contrasting paired color tablets
Readiness: Can attend to a two-object comparison.
Presentation outline: Handle tablets by their edges. / Place one tablet and find its matching color. / Lay pairs together, name colors after matching and restore.
Point of interest: Finding the same color.
Feedback / control of error: A mismatched pair can be visually compared.
What to observe: Matches before naming; note lighting and access needs.
Possible next invitation: Add more color pairs.
Safety and access: Offer accessible alternatives for visual differences; do not treat color naming as an intelligence measure.

Direct aim: Order related colors by small differences in shade.
Materials: One family of graded color tablets
Readiness: Can match similar colors and enjoys fine comparison.
Presentation outline: Place the darkest and lightest shades apart. / Select the next shade and make a continuous series. / Review the transitions and adjust if needed.
Point of interest: Very small changes in shade.
Feedback / control of error: An abrupt shade change invites comparison.
What to observe: Compares adjacent shades and revises choices.
Possible next invitation: Grade a second color family in good natural light.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Compare and match geometric outlines.
Materials: A few inset shapes with matching frames
Readiness: Can manage knobs and compare outlines.
Presentation outline: Remove one inset and trace its edge with two fingers. / Trace the matching frame and fit the inset gently. / Repeat with two or three contrasting shapes.
Point of interest: The edge and the space share an outline.
Feedback / control of error: The inset fits its matching frame.
What to observe: Tracks an edge and compares shape without forcing.
Possible next invitation: Match insets to outline cards.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Compare textures through a comfortable tactile experience.
Materials: Paired texture tablets; handwashing access
Readiness: Can choose to touch materials and communicate comfort.
Presentation outline: Explore two textures lightly with fingertips. / Compare another tablet and find the matching texture. / Pair tablets, then offer language such as rough and smooth.
Point of interest: A light touch reveals texture.
Feedback / control of error: Paired textures can be checked again by touch; some comparisons need adult discussion.
What to observe: Touch preference and ability to compare.
Possible next invitation: Order a small series from smoother to rougher.
Safety and access: Do not require blindfolding or touch. Respect sensory boundaries; check for skin irritation.

Direct aim: Match sounds through careful listening.
Materials: Paired sealed sound cylinders
Readiness: Can handle materials gently and tolerate the sounds.
Presentation outline: Shake one cylinder gently near the body, away from ears. / Listen to another and compare. / Place matching pairs together and use the set’s check marks afterward.
Point of interest: Listening to one sound at a time.
Feedback / control of error: Matching marks, if provided, check the pairing after listening.
What to observe: Auditory comparison and volume regulation.
Possible next invitation: Compare louder and softer sounds.
Safety and access: Keep containers securely sealed and volume comfortable. Offer visual or vibration alternatives for hearing access.

Direct aim: Recognize and describe familiar geometric solids.
Materials: Sphere, cube and cylinder; mat
Readiness: Interested in handling and comparing shapes.
Presentation outline: Explore one solid with hands and eyes. / Compare how another rests or rolls. / Name a small set through a three-period language lesson.
Point of interest: Flat and curved surfaces behave differently.
Feedback / control of error: The object’s movement gives feedback; names need a supportive adult check.
What to observe: Uses sensory descriptions and notices differences.
Possible next invitation: Find a corresponding shape in the room.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Build meaningful vocabulary through real conversation.
Materials: Real objects or clear photographs related to the child’s life
Readiness: Any spoken, signed or supported communication level.
Presentation outline: Invite the child to notice a real object. / Offer its precise name and pause for a response. / Expand one idea without demanding repetition.
Point of interest: A familiar object has a useful name.
Feedback / control of error: Meaningful conversation provides feedback; naming is not self-correcting.
What to observe: Initiation, vocabulary, home-language strengths and communication supports.
Possible next invitation: Make a small vocabulary basket from an interest.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Connect a small set of words with familiar objects.
Materials: Two or three already explored objects
Readiness: Attends to short interactions and can indicate a choice.
Presentation outline: Name each object simply: this is a sphere. / Ask the child to show or move a named object in varied ways. / Only when recognition is secure, invite the child to name it.
Point of interest: Moving and finding known objects.
Feedback / control of error: Adult observation guides a return to naming; do not quiz through repeated errors.
What to observe: Recognition separately from recall.
Possible next invitation: Repeat with another small vocabulary set.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Identify a beginning sound in a familiar spoken word.
Materials: Two or three familiar objects with clear starting sounds
Readiness: Understands the object names; can attend to sound play.
Presentation outline: Name the objects naturally. / Say a starting sound without adding a vowel and invite a match. / Play briefly, then use the sound in another familiar word.
Point of interest: Hearing a sound inside a spoken word.
Feedback / control of error: An adult models the sound and supports comparison.
What to observe: Sound awareness separately from letter knowledge.
Possible next invitation: Notice ending sounds after beginning sounds are secure.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Hear and sequence individual sounds in a short spoken word.
Materials: A few familiar short words; optional counters
Readiness: Can identify some individual spoken sounds.
Presentation outline: Say a short word slowly without distorting it. / Help the child listen for each sound in order. / Use one counter per heard sound and blend the word again.
Point of interest: A word can be taken apart and joined again.
Feedback / control of error: An adult checks spoken sound order; do not use letter count as a substitute.
What to observe: Sounds heard and support required.
Possible next invitation: Build the same word with a movable alphabet.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Connect a speech sound with its written form and tracing movement.
Materials: Two or three contrasting sandpaper letters
Readiness: Shows sound awareness and tolerates the texture.
Presentation outline: Trace in the direction used for writing while saying the sound. / Invite tracing with the child’s preferred hand. / Use a brief three-period lesson to revisit the sound-symbol link.
Point of interest: The movement and sound happen together.
Feedback / control of error: Texture guides tracing; an adult supports direction and sound accuracy.
What to observe: Sound-symbol link, movement and comfort.
Possible next invitation: Find a matching sound in a familiar object name.
Safety and access: Offer a smooth or visual alternative if the texture is uncomfortable. Letter forms and sounds should suit the language being taught.

Direct aim: Explore controlled lines and outlines with a comfortable drawing movement.
Materials: Inset frame; colored pencils; paper
Readiness: Can hold a drawing tool comfortably with support if needed.
Presentation outline: Stabilize a frame and trace inside its boundary. / Trace the matching inset to compare the outlines. / Fill with controlled lines, adapting length to endurance.
Point of interest: An outline closes and lines stay within a chosen shape.
Feedback / control of error: Visible lines provide feedback; comfort and movement need adult observation.
What to observe: Light pressure, bilateral coordination and endurance.
Possible next invitation: Combine two outlines for a design.
Safety and access: Avoid forced pencil grips or long repetitive tracing sessions.

Direct aim: Represent a meaningful word through selected sound symbols.
Materials: Movable alphabet; familiar objects or ideas
Readiness: Can hear several sounds and recognizes corresponding symbols.
Presentation outline: Choose a meaningful spoken word. / Say its sounds slowly and select corresponding letters. / Read the sounds together and discuss the intended word.
Point of interest: Writing an idea before pencil control is fully developed.
Feedback / control of error: The spoken word can be compared with the letters; an adult supports conventional spelling.
What to observe: Sound representation, confidence and intended meaning.
Possible next invitation: Build a phrase from a child’s own idea.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Decode a familiar-pattern word and connect it with meaning.
Materials: Decodable words using known sound-symbol patterns; objects
Readiness: Can blend sounds and knows the symbols used.
Presentation outline: Show one short word without a picture clue. / Invite sound blending, allowing processing time. / Match the decoded word to the object and discuss its meaning.
Point of interest: The printed word carries a message.
Feedback / control of error: Object matching supports meaning; an adult checks accurate decoding.
What to observe: Decoding separately from guessing from pictures.
Possible next invitation: Read a short meaningful phrase with known patterns.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Read and apply a new sound-spelling pattern.
Materials: A small matched set of phonogram cards and decodable words
Readiness: Can read simple words with known correspondences.
Presentation outline: Introduce one spelling pattern with its sound. / Read a few words using that pattern. / Sort or build words and use one in a meaningful sentence.
Point of interest: More than one letter can represent a sound.
Feedback / control of error: A checked word set and adult modeling support accuracy.
What to observe: Pattern recognition, blending and transfer.
Possible next invitation: Revisit the pattern in an appropriate decodable text.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Read a useful word while attending to its unusual spelling part.
Materials: A few useful words with untaught or unusual spellings
Readiness: Has a developing decoding foundation.
Presentation outline: Say and discuss one useful word. / Identify regular sound-spelling parts and point out the unexpected part. / Read and use it in a short phrase, then revisit later.
Point of interest: Noticing the part that needs special attention.
Feedback / control of error: A model card and adult feedback support checking.
What to observe: Recognition in a phrase, not only on an isolated card.
Possible next invitation: Find the word in a short appropriate text.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Read a short message and demonstrate its meaning through a safe action.
Materials: Simple action slips using readable words
Readiness: Can decode the words and understands the actions.
Presentation outline: Offer one short printed action privately. / Invite the child to read and carry out the safe action. / Discuss meaning, then let the child choose another slip.
Point of interest: Print can invite an action without spoken directions.
Feedback / control of error: The action can be compared with the message by child and adult.
What to observe: Comprehension beyond word pronunciation.
Possible next invitation: Write a command for a willing peer.
Safety and access: Avoid unsafe movement, food commands or actions that require unwanted touch.

Direct aim: Explore the naming function of words within meaningful phrases.
Materials: Familiar objects; phrase slips; grammar symbols if used
Readiness: Reads simple phrases and can discuss familiar objects.
Presentation outline: Read a phrase naming an object. / Explore which word names the thing and which small word helps introduce it. / Match phrases to objects and discuss the words’ jobs.
Point of interest: A word has a job in a meaningful phrase.
Feedback / control of error: Object matching and adult discussion check meaning.
What to observe: Meaningful word-function awareness rather than memorized labels.
Possible next invitation: Explore an adjective that changes which object is meant.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Read a sentence and communicate its meaning.
Materials: Short child-relevant sentences with accessible spelling patterns
Readiness: Can read phrases with growing ease.
Presentation outline: Read a short sentence together or independently. / Ask what happened, allowing spoken, drawn or acted responses. / Return to the sentence to find evidence for the response.
Point of interest: The whole message matters.
Feedback / control of error: The text and adult discussion support checking.
What to observe: Accuracy, fluency, comprehension and enjoyment separately.
Possible next invitation: Read a short connected text.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Organize and record an original story in an accessible form.
Materials: Paper; drawing tools; optional adult scribe
Readiness: Has an idea to communicate by speech, signs, drawing or print.
Presentation outline: Invite a real or imagined event. / Help arrange a beginning, a development and an ending without taking over. / Record the child’s words with permission and share the finished book.
Point of interest: An idea becomes a book another person can understand.
Feedback / control of error: The child checks whether the record expresses the intended story.
What to observe: Sequence, vocabulary, authorship and preferred communication.
Possible next invitation: Add a page or reread to a chosen listener.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Connect counted sections with a whole quantity.
Materials: Ten alternating-color number rods; rug
Readiness: Can grade lengths and is interested in counting.
Presentation outline: Build the length series with ends aligned. / Touch and count each section of a selected rod once. / Name its whole quantity and compare with another rod.
Point of interest: A quantity stays together as one rod.
Feedback / control of error: Length and colored sections support counting checks.
What to observe: One-to-one counting and quantity recognition.
Possible next invitation: Match known rods to number symbols.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Recognize and trace familiar numeral symbols.
Materials: Two or three sandpaper numerals
Readiness: Understands some spoken quantities and enjoys symbol exploration.
Presentation outline: Trace one numeral in its writing direction while naming it. / Invite the child to trace or observe. / Use a short three-period lesson with contrasting numerals.
Point of interest: Movement is connected to a number name.
Feedback / control of error: Texture guides movement; adult observation checks name and direction.
What to observe: Symbol recognition separately from counting.
Possible next invitation: Match numerals to counted quantities.
Safety and access: Provide a nontextured alternative when needed.

Direct aim: Match a known quantity with its numeral.
Materials: Number rods; corresponding numeral cards
Readiness: Knows several rod quantities and numeral names.
Presentation outline: Choose a rod and count its sections. / Find its matching numeral and place it beside the rod. / Check by recounting and compare another pair.
Point of interest: A written symbol stands for a quantity.
Feedback / control of error: Recounting sections supports a check; an adult confirms symbols.
What to observe: Quantity-symbol correspondence and self-checking.
Possible next invitation: Mix a small set of numerals and rods.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Build separate quantities and explore zero as no objects.
Materials: Spindle boxes labeled zero through nine; complete spindle set
Readiness: Counts small quantities and recognizes numerals zero to nine.
Presentation outline: Read a compartment’s numeral. / Count that many spindles into a group and place them inside. / Leave zero empty and notice whether any spindles remain.
Point of interest: Zero means no items in that compartment.
Feedback / control of error: The exact set total reveals many counting errors.
What to observe: One-to-one counting, grouping and meaning of zero.
Possible next invitation: Recheck any remaining spindles together.
Safety and access: Assess small-part safety and supervise materials appropriately.

Lesson: Cards and counters: odd and even
Direct aim: Represent quantities in pairs and notice odd/even arrangements.
Materials: Numerals one to ten; complete counter set
Readiness: Can count to ten and match quantities to symbols.
Presentation outline: Order the numerals and count counters beneath each. / Arrange counters in pairs, placing an unmatched one below. / Compare groups with and without an unmatched counter.
Point of interest: Some quantities pair completely.
Feedback / control of error: The counter arrangement makes an unmatched one visible.
What to observe: Accurate quantity and recognition of pairing.
Possible next invitation: Discuss odd and even using the arrangement.
Safety and access: Use counters suitable for the child and assess choking risk.

Direct aim: Explore units, tens, hundreds and thousands as related quantities.
Materials: Unit bead; ten bar; hundred square; thousand cube
Readiness: Understands counting to ten and can compare quantities.
Presentation outline: Explore each quantity category one at a time. / Count or compare ten of one category with one of the next. / Name the categories and invite the child to bring one.
Point of interest: Ten of a category makes one of the next.
Feedback / control of error: Material structure and guided counting support checking.
What to observe: Quantity language and comparisons before symbol demands.
Possible next invitation: Associate large number cards with the quantities.
Safety and access: Assess small-part risk. Use robust materials and close supervision as needed.

Direct aim: Connect decimal quantities with written place-value symbols.
Materials: Large number cards; golden bead quantities
Readiness: Recognizes the decimal quantity categories.
Presentation outline: Introduce category cards in a small set. / Build a quantity and choose the matching cards. / Overlay cards to form the number, then separate them to show place value.
Point of interest: A number is made from separate quantity categories.
Feedback / control of error: Comparing the bead categories with the cards supports checking.
What to observe: Place value rather than naming a long number by rote.
Possible next invitation: Read and build a different number with a zero category.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Combine two concrete quantities without exchanges.
Materials: Golden beads; number cards; trays; prepared quantities
Readiness: Can compose decimal quantities and combine small sets.
Presentation outline: Build two quantities that do not require exchanging. / Bring like categories together and count each total. / Choose result cards and describe joining the quantities.
Point of interest: Two collections become one total.
Feedback / control of error: Rebuilding and recounting check the result; an adult verifies the setup.
What to observe: Combining, category order and result explanation.
Possible next invitation: Repeat independently before introducing exchanges.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Lesson: Golden bead exchange and dynamic addition
Direct aim: Combine quantities and preserve value through decimal exchanges.
Materials: Golden beads; cards; exchange supply
Readiness: Understands static addition and ten-to-one relationships.
Presentation outline: Combine two prepared quantities. / When ten of a category accumulate, exchange them for one of the next. / Recount and represent the total with cards.
Point of interest: An exchange changes the form, not the amount.
Feedback / control of error: Compare the total before and after exchanging with adult support.
What to observe: Exchange reasoning and keeping categories aligned.
Possible next invitation: Compose another total needing one exchange.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Represent taking away and identify what remains.
Materials: Golden beads; cards; a prepared whole and amount to remove
Readiness: Understands taking away and can compose the starting quantity.
Presentation outline: Build the starting whole. / Remove the requested quantity into another space. / Count what remains and explain the change.
Point of interest: The remaining collection represents the difference.
Feedback / control of error: Put the removed amount back to check the starting whole.
What to observe: Meaning of subtraction and accurate removal.
Possible next invitation: Introduce a needed exchange only after a clear concrete foundation.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Explore multiplication through combining equal groups.
Materials: Golden beads; identical quantity trays; cards
Readiness: Can combine quantities and recognize equal groups.
Presentation outline: Prepare a small number of equal groups. / Combine like categories and find the total. / Describe the repeated equal quantity using the appropriate language.
Point of interest: Each group starts with the same amount.
Feedback / control of error: Reconstruct equal groups to check the total.
What to observe: Equal groups separately from a memorized fact.
Possible next invitation: Use another small equal-group example.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Explore division through sharing a quantity equally.
Materials: Golden beads; a divisible total; recipient markers
Readiness: Understands equal sharing and concrete quantities.
Presentation outline: Set out the recipients and the whole collection. / Share one category fairly, exchanging only with guidance if appropriate. / Compare shares and state how much each receives.
Point of interest: Each recipient receives the same amount.
Feedback / control of error: Compare shares and recombine them to check the whole.
What to observe: Fair sharing, tracking recipients and remainder awareness.
Possible next invitation: Try another exactly divisible quantity first.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Connect a group of ten and extra units with a teen symbol.
Materials: Teen boards or cards; ten bars; unit beads
Readiness: Understands ten and one-to-one counting beyond ten.
Presentation outline: Build ten and add one or more units. / Match the quantity to its teen symbol. / Count the whole and name the number without losing the group of ten.
Point of interest: A teen number contains one ten and some units.
Feedback / control of error: Compare the bar and units with the symbol; an adult checks naming.
What to observe: Teen naming, quantity and symbol as separate observations.
Possible next invitation: Compare two teen numbers.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Connect groups of tens and additional units with two-digit symbols.
Materials: Tens boards or cards; ten bars; units
Readiness: Understands a ten bar and some teen quantities.
Presentation outline: Count ten bars as tens. / Match the quantity to the appropriate tens symbol. / Add units and compose a two-digit number.
Point of interest: Tens stay grouped while units change.
Feedback / control of error: Count bars and units against the cards.
What to observe: Counting by tens and composing without rote guessing.
Possible next invitation: Build and read a child-chosen two-digit number.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Explore counting sequences and repeated equal groups.
Materials: A suitable bead chain; matching labels; long safe work space
Readiness: Counts accurately and can sustain a longer sequence.
Presentation outline: Lay out a short chain and count each bead. / Place labels at repeated group boundaries. / Review the repeating group size and connect it with equal groups.
Point of interest: A regular numerical pattern appears.
Feedback / control of error: Count back along the chain and compare labels; guided checks may be needed.
What to observe: Accurate tracking, sequence and recognition of equal groups.
Possible next invitation: Choose a longer chain when endurance and interest support it.
Safety and access: Keep walkways clear and assess bead safety.

Lesson: Fraction insets: whole and equal parts
Direct aim: Explore a whole divided into equal parts.
Materials: Fraction circles or equal-part insets
Readiness: Can compare shapes and discuss a whole.
Presentation outline: Explore a whole circle, then replace it with two equal parts. / Compare equal parts with other equal divisions. / Name simple fractions in relation to the same whole.
Point of interest: Equal parts recombine into the whole.
Feedback / control of error: Insets fill the same frame without gaps or overlaps.
What to observe: Equal partitioning and the relationship to the whole.
Possible next invitation: Compare one-half and one-fourth of the same-sized whole.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Recognize a globe as a model of Earth’s land and water.
Materials: Land-and-water globe; plain map; small land/water photos
Readiness: Interested in the world and can explore a model.
Presentation outline: Explore the globe’s land and water surfaces. / Find examples in photographs and compare them. / Explain that the globe is a small model of Earth.
Point of interest: A model represents a much larger place.
Feedback / control of error: Model and photos support comparison; adult dialogue checks meaning.
What to observe: Model understanding and land/water language.
Possible next invitation: Explore a continent globe.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Relate continent shapes on a globe and a flat map to real places.
Materials: Continent globe; puzzle map; diverse place photographs
Readiness: Understands globe as a model of Earth.
Presentation outline: Relate the flat map to the globe. / Explore and name a small number of continents. / Connect a continent to real places and varied communities.
Point of interest: A shape on the map represents real places.
Feedback / control of error: Puzzle outlines support placement; names require guided checking.
What to observe: Location, model awareness and respectful questions.
Possible next invitation: Investigate one place connected to a child’s family.
Safety and access: Present political and cultural information thoughtfully; do not equate one continent with one language or culture.

Direct aim: Compare island and lake models with real landforms.
Materials: Safe landform trays; small amount of water; photos
Readiness: Can pour with support and compare land with water.
Presentation outline: Add a little water to an island model. / Compare a lake model and notice what surrounds what. / Match each model to a real photograph and name it.
Point of interest: The surrounding material changes the landform.
Feedback / control of error: Models and photographs support checking with an adult.
What to observe: Explains what surrounds land or water.
Possible next invitation: Explore another contrasting landform pair.
Safety and access: Use shallow water under supervision and empty trays after use.

Direct aim: Use observations to explore characteristics of living things.
Materials: Photos or safely observed examples; sorting spaces
Readiness: Interested in plants, animals and everyday objects.
Presentation outline: Observe a few clear examples of living things. / Discuss growth and needs across time, not movement alone. / Sort clear examples and keep uncertain cases for inquiry.
Point of interest: Living things have needs and change over time.
Feedback / control of error: Adult-supported evidence checks the sort; a moving object is not necessarily living.
What to observe: Reasoning and questions rather than a memorized answer.
Possible next invitation: Observe a plant’s changes over several days.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Lesson: Parts and care of a plant
Direct aim: Connect plant parts with their functions and care.
Materials: Healthy non-toxic plant; plant diagram; care tools
Readiness: Can handle a plant gently.
Presentation outline: Observe roots if visible, stem and leaves without damaging them. / Name parts and connect each with a simple function. / Provide the plant’s actual care and record what changes.
Point of interest: The parts work together in a real plant.
Feedback / control of error: A diagram supports names; the plant’s condition informs care over time.
What to observe: Care decisions, vocabulary and close observation.
Possible next invitation: Draw and label the observed plant.
Safety and access: Select non-toxic species; check allergies and avoid unknown plants or soil ingestion.

Direct aim: Record actual changes in a growing seed over time.
Materials: Safe seeds; clear container; suitable growing medium; observation sheets
Readiness: Can follow a simple care routine.
Presentation outline: Prepare a few seeds using suitable growing conditions. / Observe regularly and draw what is actually visible. / Compare changes without inventing a result or fixed growth date.
Point of interest: A change can be recorded before it can be explained.
Feedback / control of error: Dated observations allow comparisons; a seed may not germinate.
What to observe: Descriptive language, patience and evidence.
Possible next invitation: Compare one carefully changed growing condition with adult guidance.
Safety and access: Do not eat experimental seeds. Check mold, allergies and small-part risks; wash hands.

Direct aim: Compare animals using a limited, accurate set of shared features.
Materials: Accurate animal pictures; small classification set
Readiness: Recognizes several animals and enjoys comparison.
Presentation outline: Compare a few animals by an observable feature. / Introduce a limited, accurate grouping and relevant vocabulary. / Discuss varied needs and habitats without treating all members as identical.
Point of interest: A grouping helps us notice shared features.
Feedback / control of error: Reliable reference pictures and adult review check the grouping.
What to observe: Uses evidence and recognizes exceptions when introduced.
Possible next invitation: Investigate one animal in more detail.
Safety and access: Do not bring unknown wildlife into the classroom or require animal handling.

Direct aim: Make and test predictions about magnetic attraction.
Materials: Large encased magnet; safe test objects; two trays
Readiness: Can follow handling limits and make a prediction.
Presentation outline: Predict whether one object will be attracted. / Test it slowly and observe without changing the claim afterward. / Group results and try another object of a different material.
Point of interest: A prediction may differ from the result.
Feedback / control of error: The test outcome is observable; repeat to confirm.
What to observe: Prediction, actual result and descriptive language.
Possible next invitation: Compare different safe metal objects.
Safety and access: Use a large, intact encased magnet under direct supervision. Never use loose high-powered magnets or objects that can be swallowed.

Direct aim: Record and compare daily observations of local weather.
Materials: Window or safe outdoor space; weather symbols; dated journal
Readiness: Can make a brief daily observation.
Presentation outline: Look at the actual sky and surroundings. / Record what is observed using a drawing, symbol or dictated note. / Compare records after several days without predicting a fixed pattern.
Point of interest: A record helps remember yesterday accurately.
Feedback / control of error: The journal can be compared with current observations; past entries are evidence, not forecasts.
What to observe: Observation separate from prediction.
Possible next invitation: Compare clothing choices with the actual conditions.
Safety and access: Follow outdoor weather, air quality and sun-safety procedures.

Direct aim: Arrange personally meaningful events in a sequence.
Materials: Optional family-approved photos or child drawings; timeline strip
Readiness: Interested in personal history; comfortable sharing.
Presentation outline: Invite the child to select events they want to share. / Arrange a few events in meaningful order. / Discuss what has changed and what remains important.
Point of interest: A sequence represents the passage of time.
Feedback / control of error: Family information and the child’s account support checking.
What to observe: Temporal words and respect for different family stories.
Possible next invitation: Make a timeline of a classroom project.
Safety and access: Participation and family photos are optional. Respect adoption, loss, privacy and varied family structures.

Direct aim: Explore real community roles without stereotypes.
Materials: Local photographs; books; optional invited visitor
Readiness: Interested in how people help a community.
Presentation outline: Ask what the child has noticed people doing. / Explore several real roles using inclusive examples. / Connect a role with tools, choices and ways children can ask for help.
Point of interest: Work has a purpose in the community.
Feedback / control of error: Authentic accounts and reliable books support checking.
What to observe: Questions, vocabulary and avoiding stereotypes.
Possible next invitation: Prepare respectful questions for a visitor.
Safety and access: Follow visitor and safeguarding procedures; do not imply every uniformed person is automatically a safe contact.

Direct aim: Explore a family’s shared experience with respect and curiosity.
Materials: Family-volunteered stories, music, objects or books
Readiness: Shows interest; families choose what and whether to share.
Presentation outline: Invite a specific contribution without asking one family to represent a whole culture. / Explore the item and its meaning in that family’s own words. / Record questions and similarities without ranking traditions.
Point of interest: People within the same culture can have different experiences.
Feedback / control of error: The contributing family’s account and reliable sources guide interpretation.
What to observe: Respectful questions and language about similarities and differences.
Possible next invitation: Explore another family’s perspective with consent.
Safety and access: Do not use sacred items as dress-up props, require cultural disclosure or assign a child the role of cultural spokesperson.

Direct aim: Make and communicate original drawing choices.
Materials: Accessible drawing tools; paper; workspace
Readiness: Interested in making marks.
Presentation outline: Show safe care of one drawing tool. / Invite the child to choose marks, colors and subject. / Offer descriptive feedback and let the child decide whether to keep or share.
Point of interest: The child makes meaningful choices.
Feedback / control of error: The child’s intention guides revision; there is no model to copy exactly.
What to observe: Choices, movement and the child’s own account.
Possible next invitation: Offer a different drawing medium.
Safety and access: Use intact, child-sized materials. Supervise according to the child and the activity.

Direct aim: Use safe cutting and joining techniques in an original composition.
Materials: Child-sized scissors; paper strips; paste; backing paper
Readiness: Can follow scissor safety with appropriate support.
Presentation outline: Show how to carry, hold and close scissors safely. / Offer short strips to cut and a choice of placement. / Demonstrate a small amount of paste and invite an original composition.
Point of interest: Cut pieces can be arranged in many ways.
Feedback / control of error: The child decides the design; adult feedback supports safe tool use.
What to observe: Two-hand coordination, safe handling and artistic choices.
Possible next invitation: Offer wider strips or a chosen simple line.
Safety and access: Supervise scissors; use adaptive tools as needed and check paste ingredients.

Direct aim: Explore and shape a modeling material with chosen techniques.
Materials: Non-toxic modeling material; mat; simple blunt tools
Readiness: Can handle material safely and does not mouth it.
Presentation outline: Show pressing, rolling and pinching as options. / Invite the child to explore and create without a required product. / Clean tools and hands and store the material correctly.
Point of interest: Hands change the material’s form.
Feedback / control of error: The child compares the form with their intention.
What to observe: Hand strength, sensory preference and chosen techniques.
Possible next invitation: Make a form from an observation or story.
Safety and access: Check ingredients and allergies; do not use food-based dough where it creates a risk. Supervise small pieces.

Direct aim: Notice, repeat or create a short rhythmic pattern.
Materials: Voice, clapping or a safe quiet percussion instrument
Readiness: Can participate comfortably through movement, sound or observation.
Presentation outline: Offer a short comfortable rhythm. / Invite an echo or an alternative accessible response. / Let the child offer a pattern for a willing adult or peer.
Point of interest: A pattern can be heard, felt or seen.
Feedback / control of error: Listen or watch together; participation is not scored for perfection.
What to observe: Pattern noticing, turn taking and sound comfort.
Possible next invitation: Combine a rhythm with a familiar song.
Safety and access: Keep sound levels comfortable and offer a quiet opt-out.

Direct aim: Explore contrasting pitches and musical response.
Materials: Voice or tuned child-appropriate instrument; two contrasting pitches
Readiness: Enjoys listening and can choose whether to join.
Presentation outline: Offer two comfortable contrasting pitches. / Invite listening, gesture or vocal exploration. / Sing a short familiar phrase and let the child choose a way to respond.
Point of interest: Sounds can be higher or lower.
Feedback / control of error: Comparison and adult modeling support listening; singing accuracy is not a judgment of musical worth.
What to observe: Listening, preference and willing participation.
Possible next invitation: Explore another short melody.
Safety and access: Avoid loud or strained singing; respect hearing and communication differences.

Lesson: Walking the line and expressive movement
Direct aim: Practice safe controlled and expressive movement with appropriate access.
Materials: Clear floor line; optional gentle music
Readiness: Can move in the space with safe support.
Presentation outline: Demonstrate careful walking with awareness of the space. / Invite chosen movement at a comfortable pace without requiring heel-to-toe perfection. / Offer a pause, notice others and return the space to order.
Point of interest: Movement can be controlled and expressive.
Feedback / control of error: Balance and spatial feedback guide adjustments.
What to observe: Coordination, self-regulation and participation choices.
Possible next invitation: Offer a simple movement pattern or accessible seated alternative.
Safety and access: Clear the floor, avoid slippery surfaces and provide mobility adaptations without penalty.
